# Renders the target figure shown further down this page — you'll do the actual
# work inside your day2-projects/ folder, not here. This cell is not step zero.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
data(penguins)
penguins <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep), !is.na(body_mass))
Starting point: a shipped set of pages. You don’t start from a blank folder. Open your day2-projects/ folder from the exercises download (double-click day2-projects.Rproj, see the Setup page). It holds two content pages that already render on their own but are not yet a project:
Render one page to confirm it works: quarto render analysis.qmd gives a normal HTML page (analysis.html right next to its source), since the folder isn’t a project yet. Your job across the two challenges is to make it a site, then ship it. Everything you render lands inside day2-projects/. There’s no project folder above it, so nothing redirects your output. A finished reference is in solutions/day2/ if you get stuck or fall behind.

title: Quarto projects — Lab
text:
1 Website Challenge

Goal: turn the day2-projects/ pages into a navigable, branded website that renders locally to a _site/ folder.







Note Tasks





In day2-projects/, create a _quarto.yml that declares the project and a website with navigation:
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: _site
website:
  title: "Penguin Lab"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: analysis.qmd
        text: Analysis
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
Render the whole folder: from inside day2-projects/, run quarto render (or quarto preview). Because a _quarto.yml is now present, Quarto treats the folder as one project and builds both pages into _site/.
Brand it. Add a day2-projects/_brand.yml so the site shares one palette:
color:
  palette:
    teal: "#4C979F"
  primary: teal
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Albert Sans
      source: google
  base:
    family: Albert Sans
Re-render. The navbar and headings pick up the palette automatically.
(stretch) Two things make the within-page versus across-page rule concrete. First, on analysis.qmd, drop @tbl-means into a sentence: it resolves to Table 1 because the reference and its table share one page (exactly as yesterday). Second, notice index.qmd already links to the analysis with a plain Markdown link, [analysis](analysis.qmd). That’s deliberate, because across pages there is no auto-numbering (a book feature, not a website one), so a plain link is how you connect website pages.




 Quarto docs
Websites · Brand






Note You should see



A day2-projects/_site/ folder with two linked pages and a top navbar (Home · Analysis); after the brand step, the navbar and headings turn teal with Albert Sans (the plot keeps its default species colors, since branding an R plot is a separate brand.yml-package step, out of scope today). If you did the stretch, the analysis page also shows a live Table 1 reference (from @tbl-means) and the home page carries a plain link into the analysis. Opening _site/index.html shows the home page; the navbar moves you to the analysis page, whose figure is:










Figure 1: The analysis page’s figure: body mass by species.











TipHint






The _quarto.yml must sit inside day2-projects/: Quarto uses the nearest _quarto.yml as the project root, so this makes day2-projects/ its own project. There’s no _quarto.yml in any folder above it, so nothing else can claim your pages.
navbar: items are href + text. sidebar: { contents: auto } builds a menu from the folder’s files instead.
_brand.yml is auto-discovered at the project root: no header line needed, just re-render.
quarto render with no file argument builds the whole project; quarto render index.qmd builds one page.




The solutions/day2/ folder is a reference, not a checklist. The complete, known-good project lives there in your exercises download: open it to compare your _quarto.yml / _brand.yml, or copy it wholesale if you fell behind.

title: Quarto projects — Lab
text:
2 Ship it Challenge

Goal: make the project’s builds reproducible with freeze, then render it to a publishable _site/ folder. (Publishing to Pages is the watch-me demo. You produce the folder.)







NoteStarting point



Keep going with your Website Challenge day2-projects/. If you didn’t finish it, open the ready-made solutions/day2/ project (a complete Part-1 site) and do the steps below in there.








Note Tasks





Add freeze to your project’s _quarto.yml so unchanged pages aren’t re-executed on every build:
execute:
  freeze: auto      # re-execute a document only when its own source changes
See the skip. Run quarto render once (the code runs; _freeze/ is written). Run quarto render again without editing: the R cell is skipped, its result reused from _freeze/ (the log shows no compute). For a visible tell, drop a cell with cat(format(Sys.time())) on analysis.qmd: on the frozen second render the printed timestamp does not change: a pass/fail you can see, not just an absence in the log. Now change the plot’s code on analysis.qmd and re-render: only that page re-runs (and the timestamp finally ticks).
Find the shipped site under _site/: that folder is what you publish. Point any static host at it (GitHub Pages, Netlify, an internal server).
(note, not a step) renv::snapshot() writes an renv.lock that pins the packages: the second reproducibility leg, so a teammate (or CI) rebuilds the same environment.




 Quarto docs
Freeze · Publishing






Note You should see



On the second render (no edits between them), the log shows the R cell skipped (reused from _freeze/), and the cat(format(Sys.time())) line prints the same time it did on the first render. That frozen timestamp (and the quiet log) is exactly what lets CI render the site with no R at all. Edit a page’s code, and only that page re-runs, its timestamp finally advancing.








TipHint






freeze: auto re-executes a document when its source changes (prose or code) and reuses _freeze/ when it hasn’t, so an unchanged page never re-runs. freeze: true goes further: never re-execute on a project build (the CI mode).
Frozen results live in _freeze/: commit that folder so CI can render without R.
output-dir (default _site) is the whole deliverable: publish the folder, don’t rebuild on the host.










NoteSolution: the freeze block and the render flow





Add to your project’s _quarto.yml:
execute:
  freeze: auto
An optional visible tell: put this on analysis.qmd. A frozen render reuses the old value, so the printed time stays put.
cat(format(Sys.time()))
From inside your project folder (day2-projects/):
quarto render     # 1st build: runs the code, writes _freeze/ and _site/
quarto render     # 2nd build, no edits: the cell is skipped, timestamp unchanged
# then change the plot code on analysis.qmd and render again: only that page re-runs (time ticks)
To publish, point a host at _site/ (the watch-me demo: quarto publish gh-pages, auth pre-flighted).

title: Quarto projects — Lab
text:
3 Troubleshooting






Tip If a render misbehaves






Rendered, but can’t find the HTML? Before you add _quarto.yml, a single-page render writes the HTML next to its source in day2-projects/. Once _quarto.yml is present, a project render collects both pages under day2-projects/_site/. Look in those two places.
YAML is indentation-sensitive. If rendering fails before any code runs, check _quarto.yml for stray spaces, tabs, or unmatched quotes.
“No project” / pages don’t link? The _quarto.yml must be inside day2-projects/, and href: paths are relative to the source folder, not _site/.
Brand not applied? _brand.yml must be in day2-projects/ (the project root). Re-render after adding it. For plots, the palette needs library(brand.yml) + theme_brand_ggplot2() (the file alone doesn’t reach ggplot).
A cross-reference shows ?@…? The cell label must start fig-/tbl-/eq- and be unique, and remember it only resolves within one page on a website.
Freeze didn’t skip the cell? It skips only when the source is unchanged since the last build: any edit (prose or code) re-runs that page. Delete _freeze/ to force a clean rebuild.
Missing package? install.packages("<name>") (or renv::restore()) and render again.

title: Quarto projects
text:
Learning Outcomes
Yesterday: one .qmd → a branded PDF. Today, the other axis: one file to many. You will be able to:

structure several .qmd into one Quarto project with shared config (_quarto.yml);
build a navigable, branded website — within-page cross-references, reproducible builds;
publish it, and explain how freeze lets it rebuild without re-running R.

By the end: the same penguins data, a fresh set of pages grown into a website your team can publish.


Frame: Day 1 took one .qmd all the way to a branded PDF. Day 2 is the other axis — one file to many, tied together by config, then shipped. This is the machinery behind your team project’s site.

title: Quarto projects
text:
How today works
Same shape as yesterday: two rounds of watch → follow along → your turn, each ending in a ~45-minute Challenge in the lab (solutions folded in), with a break between the rounds.
Watch for the Follow along / Your turn callouts: they flag every switch.


Quick recap, don’t re-teach — they saw this shape yesterday. Same two rounds; the Follow along / Your turn callouts flag every switch. One breath, then into Part 1.

title: Quarto projects
text:
Why a project?







Follow along


Open your editor: from here we build one project together.




One .qmd renders alone. A project is a folder Quarto treats as one unit (shared config, one build, one output folder):




_quarto.yml

# at the project root
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: _site  # everything renders here
format:
  html:
    theme: [default, custom.scss]



quarto render builds the whole folder, not one file.
Header options set once apply to every page.
output-dir — the folder the built site lands in (_site by default). Publish that.





Say: “Day 1 was one file. Today: many files, one project. Open your editor — we build one together.”
Do: show a minimal _quarto.yml — project: type: website + output-dir. “This folder is now one unit; render builds all of it, not one file.”
Say (relevance): the team project is many pages — this is how they connect.



Quarto uses the nearest _quarto.yml up the tree as the project root: you add one to day2-projects/, and nothing sits above it, so that folder is your project.

title: Quarto projects
text:
Directory metadata — _metadata.yml
Yesterday a header set the defaults and a cell overrode them. _metadata.yml is that same idea, one scope wider: options for every page in a folder, so you don’t repeat them in each header:


analysis/_metadata.yml

# applies to every .qmd in analysis/
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true

Same narrow-wins rule, now across files: document header > _metadata.yml > _quarto.yml. Set defaults wide, override narrow.



Callback (don’t re-teach): they learned header-vs-cell precedence yesterday (#execution). Don’t re-derive “defaults wide, override narrow” — just widen it to the file/folder/project scope.
Say: “Same rule as yesterday’s header-beats-nothing / cell-beats-header — now a folder file sits between the page and the project.”



Today’s lab project is flat (a couple of pages at the root), so there’s no folder to scope. Reach for _metadata.yml when a subfolder of pages shares options.

title: Quarto projects
text:
Websites — pages & navigation
You already set type: website, which makes the folder a site: its pages share one navbar and sidebar. You describe that navigation once, and Quarto builds it:


_quarto.yml

website:
  title: "Penguin Lab"
  # top bar — one entry per page
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: analysis.qmd
        text: Analysis
  # side menu, built from the files
  sidebar:
    contents: auto


contents: auto even builds the sidebar from the folder, so you don’t hand-list pages.



Do: add the website: block live — navbar + sidebar — render, show the nav appear.
Say: “You declare the nav once: the navbar you list, the sidebar contents: auto builds from the files — Quarto generates both.”
Say (sets up next slide): “each page renders on its own — that independence is exactly why cross-refs behave differently across pages.”
Helpers: flag the classic trap now — links are relative to the source, not _site — so they meet it before the lab.




Listings turn a folder of pages into an auto-generated index (a blog, a gallery of reports) via listing: on a page. One slide’s worth, more in the linked resources.

title: Quarto projects
text:
Cross-references across a project







Eyes up — not a live Follow along


The next few slides are concept, no need to type along.




Within one page, @fig-, @tbl-, @eq- resolve to a numbered, linked reference, exactly as on Day 1. (Section headings work the same way with @sec-.)

Across different website pages, they do not auto-number: a website renders each page on its own, so link between pages with ordinary Markdown links and the navbar/sidebar instead:
See the [analysis page](analysis.qmd) for the model.







Project-wide numbering is a book


If you need “Figure 3.2” to resolve across chapters, that’s type: book: Quarto renders a book as one unit with global numbering. A website keeps per-page numbering.






Pre-flight (not spoken): if unsure on your installed Quarto, test one cross-page @fig- before the session — historically a website does not resolve it. Keep that check off the slide.

title: Quarto projects
text:
One brand → the whole project: _brand.yml
You wrote _brand.yml yesterday to brand one Typst PDF. Drop that same file at the project root and Quarto auto-discovers it (no header line, no per-page config):




_brand.yml

color:
  palette:
    teal: "#4C979F"
  primary: teal
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Albert Sans
      source: google
  base:
    family: Albert Sans



Every page and every deck inherits it from that one root file, so you never name it in a page.
Add a page tomorrow? Branded on render, nothing to wire up.
Need an exception? brand: false opts a page out; brand: other.yml points it elsewhere.




Callback (don’t re-derive): they built this file yesterday for the PDF. Today’s new angle is scale — one root file themes the whole multi-page project. Widen the scope; don’t re-teach the file.
Do: show the site before / after dropping _brand.yml at the root — navbar + headings go teal in one re-render.
Say: “You wrote this yesterday. Put it at the project root and every page and deck inherits it — brand once, not per file.”
R plots (only if asked): a plot still needs theme_brand_ggplot2() — same as yesterday; the lab’s stretch covers it.
Escape hatch (if asked): brand: false opts a page out; brand: other.yml points it elsewhere — the default brands everything, these are the overrides.
Precision: “every page/deck” = every supported-format output (html, revealjs, typst, dashboard); an unsupported format just isn’t branded — don’t say “every output”.
Placement: this is Part-1 project config, not the Part-2 tail.
Helpers: the lab installs brand.yml with install.packages() (not pak).

title: Quarto projects
text:
Your turn







Your turn — ~45 min, then a break


Head to the Lab and the Website Challenge: turn a set of .qmd into a navigable, branded website: _quarto.yml, a navbar, and the shared brand. ~45 min, then a break, back after.




You can now structure files into a branded, navigable website. After the break we make its builds reproducible and ship it.


Say (handoff): “Over to you — Website Challenge: _quarto.yml, a navbar, the shared brand. ~45 min, then we break — back at 15:30. Helpers are around.”
Helpers: first thing to check — are they working inside day2-projects/ with their new _quarto.yml, so quarto render builds the project (not a stray single page)? (Secondary: page links are source-relative, not _site.) Anyone behind can open the shipped solutions/day2/ — a finished Part-1 site — and start Part 2 clean.

title: Quarto projects
section: Freeze — don’t re-run the slow stuff
text:
Freeze — don’t re-run the slow stuff







Follow along


Back in your project’s _quarto.yml.




Day 1 I teased freeze: here’s the full story. Compute can be slow: you don’t want every prose edit to re-run a 20-minute model fit. Two tools, easily confused:

cache — the compute engine’s cache, not Quarto’s: it defers to knitr (R) / Jupyter Cache. Per-cell, kept until that cell’s code changes, and it works in a single document.
freeze — Quarto’s own switch, not about compute: it sets when a document re-executes. Project-only: rendering one file always runs it. Results live in _freeze/, refreshed only when its source changes. Commit it and CI (the automated build) rebuilds with no R at all.


# _quarto.yml
execute:
  freeze: auto        # re-execute a document only when its source changes
That’s freeze: auto, the sane setting to adopt: a page re-runs only when its own source changes. freeze: true hands you full control instead → next slide.


Say (motivation): “Compute can be slow — you don’t want a prose typo to re-run a 20-minute model fit.” (Localize to the room: a sequence alignment, a long MCMC, a big simulation.)
Do: the contrast is the point — cache = the engine’s cache (knitr for R / Jupyter Cache), per-cell, works in a single doc; freeze = Quarto’s switch, project-only, re-executes a doc only when its source changes. (Verified vs quarto.org docs/projects/code-execution.html.) Protect this distinction.
Do: show freeze: auto in _quarto.yml; “re-runs a page only when that page changed.”
If asked — why not just cache everything? cache is per-cell and can go stale across a shared repo; freeze commits whole-document results for reproducible, R-free CI rebuilds. Different jobs.
Say (payoff): commit _freeze/ and CI (a build that runs on every push) rebuilds the site with no R at all.
Teaser: the next slide is freeze: true — the render-on-demand workflow.

title: Quarto projects
section: The freeze workflow — you hold the trigger
text:
The freeze workflow — you hold the trigger
With freeze: true, a project build never runs R: it always reuses _freeze/. You refresh a page only when you choose to, by rendering that one file (a single-file render always executes):


_quarto.yml

execute:
  freeze: true

quarto render analysis.qmd     # runs the code, rewrites _freeze/ — commit it with your change

The loop: edit a page → render that one file → commit _freeze/. The project build and CI stay R-free: only the page you touched recomputes. That’s exactly how quarto.org itself is built.


freeze: auto instead lets the build recompute any changed (or not-yet-frozen) page. Convenient, but true keeps the trigger in your hands.


Anchor (real): quarto.org runs freeze: true — verified in quarto-dev/quarto-web/_quarto.yml; contributors render the changed file locally and commit _freeze/, enforced by a check-freeze.sh git hook — the same discipline this workshop repo uses.
Say: “true = the build never runs R; you decide when a page recomputes, by rendering it directly.”
Do: edit a cell on analysis.qmd → quarto render analysis.qmd → show _freeze/ change + the timestamp tick; a full project render leaves it untouched.
Contrast (lab uses auto): auto = the build recomputes changed pages for you (the sane setting, what the lab sets); true = deterministic CI + manual refresh (the CI mode).
If asked: a production render profile can set freeze: false to force a full re-execution.

title: Quarto projects
text:
Reproducibility has two legs
freeze pins the results. It doesn’t pin what produced them (the package versions):



freeze → _freeze/ — “don’t re-run the slow compute.”
renv.lock → “pin the packages, so the team rebuilds the same environment.”


renv::init()       # once, to start tracking
renv::snapshot()   # write renv.lock
renv::restore()    # rebuild the same env

Together: a colleague (or CI) rebuilds the same site, with or without re-running the analysis.


Timing: renv is the first thing to drop if short on time — the cache-vs-freeze contrast is the point of this beat, protect that.
Say: “freeze pins the results; renv.lock pins what produced them — the package versions. You want both.”

title: Quarto projects
text:
Publishing
The hands-on part is small: render, then point a host at output-dir.
quarto render              # builds the whole project into _site/

Push _site/ to any static host — GitHub Pages, Netlify, an internal server.
quarto publish gh-pages and GitHub Actions automate it, rendering from the committed _freeze/ with no R needed in CI.








Watch-me — not a live Your turn


You do the render + output-dir half; I’ll show the publish step on a ready-made repo. It needs a GitHub login and builds asynchronously (push, then wait for the green check).






Frame (why watch-me — don’t narrate the logistics): a live publish gh-pages across 40 laptops means GitHub auth and a repo each — a lot of per-person setup for one demo, and Pages/Actions rebuilds asynchronously (push, then wait for the green check), so there’s nothing synchronous to watch anyway. Foreground the CI story; keep auth off the hands-on path.
Say (keep these distinct): “quarto publish gh-pages renders here on my machine and pushes the result; GitHub Actions is the path that rebuilds from the committed _freeze/ with no R on the runner.”
Do (if demoing live): state the auth prerequisite first (GitHub login + a repo); otherwise just show the green check on the pre-provisioned repo.

title: Quarto projects
text:
Your turn







Your turn — regroup in ~45 min


Back to the Lab, the Ship it Challenge: render your project to _site/ and open it: a publishable folder. (Publishing to Pages is the watch-me demo.)






Say (handoff): “Last part — Ship it Challenge: render your project to _site/ and open it, a publishable folder. Publishing to Pages is my watch-me demo, not your job. ~45 min; helpers are around.”
Helpers: the tell that freeze is working — the second project render doesn’t re-execute the page at all (no chunk output scrolls by); the compute is served from _freeze/. Behind? Open the shipped solutions/day2/ project and start from there.

title: Quarto projects
Quarto projects
text:
Demos (if time)
Extra topics:

Book versus website — ~90% shared machinery. Pick a book when you need one linear read with global numbering, a website otherwise. (1 decision, not a new toolset.)
Dashboards — format: dashboard arranges plots/tables/valueboxes into a static layout (rows, columns, cards) to share results with a collaborator who won’t open R. See one (static, no server).
Interactivity — an htmlwidget (plotly, leaflet) is pure R and self-contained. OJS (Observable JS, a browser-side, non-R path) and Shinylive (Shiny running in the browser, no server) are links, not live builds.



Timing: cut-able tail — trim from the bottom if under ~5 min left; all watch-me, nothing built live.
Do: for the dashboard, open the [See one] link and name the four regions — two valueboxes across the top, a card with the boxplot, and a two-tab panel (the whole layout model: rows / columns / cards / valueboxes / tabsets).

text:
Thank you!
Questions?
Learn more: Projects · Websites · Freeze · Publishing

Slides + lab: this site · Christophe Dervieux · GitHub @cderv · cderv@posit.co

title: Setup
text: You need a working R + Quarto toolchain and an editor. Everything below is standard. If you already render Quarto documents from R, you are ready.

title: Setup
text:
Software

R ≥ 4.5.0. The running dataset (penguins) ships in base R only since 4.5 (check with R.version.string). The exercises use the base-R names (bill_len, bill_dep, …), so R ≥ 4.5 is the smoothest path. If you truly can’t upgrade, see the fallback below.
Quarto ≥ 1.9. Check with quarto --version and get it from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/. (1.9 is required: the Typst margin/article layout we use on Day 1 landed in 1.9.)
An editor with Quarto support — Positron, VS Code (+ the Quarto extension), or RStudio. All work, and we drive Quarto from the command line too (quarto preview / quarto render), so the editor is your choice.







Tip



Typst (the modern PDF path we use on Day 1) ships inside Quarto, so there is nothing extra to install and no LaTeX to set up.








WarningStuck on R < 4.5? (dataset fallback)





The exercises assume base R’s penguins. If you genuinely can’t get to R ≥ 4.5, install palmerpenguins and rename its columns to the base-R names the material uses, so every snippet works unchanged:
# install.packages("palmerpenguins")
library(dplyr)
penguins <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  rename(
    bill_len    = bill_length_mm,
    bill_dep    = bill_depth_mm,
    flipper_len = flipper_length_mm,
    body_mass   = body_mass_g
  )
Run this once at the top of a document (or your session) before the exercise code. Upgrading R is still the cleaner path if you can.

title: Setup
text:
Get the materials
The hands-on files live in a small exercises folder (the top raukr-2026-quarto-exercises folder): the starter documents, the reference solutions, and the citation assets (references.bib, apa.csl). The easiest way to get it is use_course() from R. No git, no GitHub account, nothing to unzip by hand, and the same on Windows, macOS, and Linux:
# install.packages("usethis")   # once, if you don't have it
usethis::use_course("cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises")
What it does:

picks a sensible spot (your Desktop by default) and prints where it’s about to download. To put it elsewhere, cancel and re-run with a path, e.g. use_course("cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises", destdir = "~/projects").
downloads a ZIP and unpacks it for you into a folder called raukr-2026-quarto-exercises (it prints the exact path). It then asks “Shall we delete the ZIP file?”. Keep it (say No): it’s your one-click reset (see below).
opens the folder — a new RStudio session, or the folder in Positron / VS Code. If it doesn’t pop open, open the folder it printed yourself.







ImportantWhich folder to open — and when



use_course() drops you in the top folder (raukr-2026-quarto-exercises). Do the next two steps (R packages and Check) from there, now, before the session.
When the session starts, open the day folder for that day, not the top folder:

Day 1 → open day1-intro/ (double-click day1-intro.Rproj).
Day 2 → open day2-projects/ (double-click day2-projects.Rproj).

Each day folder is its own working directory with its own brand and assets, so your renders land right next to your files (there’s no project folder above them to capture the output). One download covers both days. The reference answers are in solutions/day1/ and solutions/day2/ at the top folder (try first).








TipReset without losing work (no git needed)





If an attempt goes wrong, get a fresh copy of the day folder (don’t unzip over your working copy):

re-run usethis::use_course("cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises"): it makes a new, numbered folder and leaves your old attempt untouched; or
unzip the ZIP you kept to a new location.

If use_course() can’t reach GitHub (blocked network / firewall), use the browser: the green Code ▸ Download ZIP button on https://github.com/cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises, then unzip.

title: Setup
text:
R packages
The exercises use nine R packages. The simplest path is a plain install into your R library (it works no matter which day folder you open):
install.packages(c(
  "dplyr", "ggplot2", "gt", "ggokabeito",   # content + a color-blind-safe scale
  "brand.yml", "ggrepel", "prismatic",      # R-side branding for the Typst payoff
  "knitr", "rmarkdown"                      # the engine every .qmd with R code needs
))
Or with pak, which installs the same list in parallel, prefers binaries, and sorts out system dependencies for you:
# install.packages("pak")   # once, if you don't have it
pak::pak(c(
  "dplyr", "ggplot2", "gt", "ggokabeito",
  "brand.yml", "ggrepel", "prismatic",
  "knitr", "rmarkdown"
))






NotePrefer pinned versions? (optional, renv)





The exercises ship an renv.lock recording exact package versions. From the top raukr-2026-quarto-exercises folder (where renv.lock sits):
# install.packages("renv")   # if you don't have it
renv::restore()
renv builds a project-local library at that top folder, which R activates only when you work from that top folder, not when you open a day folder. So if you go the renv route, render from the top folder too. Otherwise the plain install.packages() above (into your regular library) is the simpler path that works in any folder. Pick one, you don’t need both.

title: Setup
text:
Check your setup
The exercises folder ships a one-shot check. From the top raukr-2026-quarto-exercises folder, run:
source("00-check-setup.R")
It verifies R ≥ 4.5, Quarto ≥ 1.9, the nine packages, and the base-R penguins data, then renders the Day-1 Typst sample (day1-intro/sample-typst.qmd). That proves the knitr + Typst chain end-to-end and caches the brand’s Google fonts (Albert Sans / Fira Mono), so your first render in the session is instant instead of pausing to download them. Every line should read [ok].






TipPrefer to check by hand?





The one command that proves the toolchain is quarto check. It covers the knitr engine too (the knitr + rmarkdown packages a .qmd with R code needs): it reports your Quarto version and renders a small knitr test document (look for Checking Knitr engine render......OK). If you see rmarkdown: (None), your R packages aren’t installed yet, so do the R packages step and re-run. Then confirm the R side:
R.version.string                          # want >= 4.5.0
"penguins" %in% ls("package:datasets")    # want TRUE on R >= 4.5
And pre-warm the fonts once by rendering the sample yourself: quarto render day1-intro/sample-typst.qmd.

title: Introduction to Quarto
Introduction to Quarto
Introduction to Quarto
Introduction to Quarto
text:
How it all works
quarto render report.qmd runs your code, then hands Markdown to Pandoc:



Frame: for R, the knitr engine runs your chunks — the same engine as R Markdown. Your .Rmd still renders as-is; knitr::convert_chunk_header() moves it to .qmd cell options when you’re ready.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Anatomy of a .qmd
Three parts: a YAML header, Markdown prose, and executable code cells.
---
title: "A penguin story"
format: html
---

We measured **`{r} nrow(penguins)`** penguins.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bill
#| fig-cap: "Bill length versus depth"
ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep, color = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

Cell options use the #| “hash-pipe”: one option per line, YAML-valued. Native from the start.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Markdown & content — think in deltas







Follow along


Open your editor and render as we go. From here on we’re building one document together. Every follow-along cell assumes this setup, so run it first:




library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
data(penguins)                                     # base R ≥ 4.5 — the dataset is zero-install
penguins <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep))
You already know Markdown. Quarto adds the research-writing pieces:

figures & tables with captions, from code;
cross-references — @fig-bill, @tbl-summary, @eq-ratio;
math — inline $…$ and display $$…$$;
inline code — report numbers from the data;
callouts — note / tip / warning / caution / important.



Say: “From here we build one document together — render as we go.”
Do: run the setup block first (libraries + penguins); every follow-along cell assumes it, so if it’s skipped the first figure cell errors.
Frame: the list is deltas over the Markdown they already know — not a Markdown lesson.
Timing: this + the next four slides (Figures / Tables & math / Callouts / Inline code) are the live build, ~8–10 min total. One point per slide; don’t polish plots.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Figures & cross-references
A labeled code cell becomes a numbered, referenceable figure:


ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_len, bill_dep,
                     color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)",
       y = "Bill depth (mm)")








Figure 1: Bill length versus depth, by species.





Refer to it in prose with @fig-bill → renders as “Figure 1”, a live link. Labels must start with fig- / tbl- / eq- to be cross-referenceable.
#| fig-alt is the figure’s alt text (the description screen readers announce). Add it to every figure. (#| output-location: column is slide-only: a revealjs placement, not article layout.)


Do: add #| label: fig-bill + #| fig-cap to the plot cell, render, show the auto-number appear.
Say: “A labeled cell becomes a numbered figure; @fig-bill in prose is a live link.”
Say (trap): the label must start fig-/tbl-/eq-, or the ref renders a stray ?@.
Do: point at output-location: column — a revealjs cell option that puts the plot in a column beside the code on this slide. (Presentation output-placement — not the article margin layout on the Layouts slide, which doesn’t apply to revealjs.)

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Tables
gt (or knitr::kable) turns a data frame into a table; a #| label: tbl- makes it referenceable.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Mean bill length per species."
penguins |>
  summarise(bill = mean(bill_len), .by = species) |>
  gt() |> fmt_number(bill, decimals = 1)
```



Table 1: Mean bill length per species.









species
bill




Adelie
38.8


Gentoo
47.5


Chinstrap
48.8










Then refer to it in prose with @tbl-summary (same mechanic as figures).


Do: show the gt cell with #| label: tbl-summary, render, point at the auto-number.
Say: “Same mechanic as figures — a tbl- label makes it referenceable; gt or knitr::kable, your call.”
Timing: the table is the must-keep; the Math slide is the trim point if Part 1 is tight.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Math
Display math with a label is cross-referenceable too:
$$
\text{ratio} = \frac{\text{bill_len}}{\text{bill_dep}}
$$ {#eq-ratio}
renders as Equation 1 below:
\[
\text{ratio} = \frac{\text{bill_len}}{\text{bill_dep}}
\tag{1}\]


Do: show the display-math block with {#eq-ratio}, then the rendered, numbered equation.
Say: “Same mechanic again — an eq- label makes the equation referenceable.”
Say (trap): inside bare $$…$$ an underscore can trigger a subscript (or an error) depending on the math renderer — escape it as bill\_len (the lab warns about this too).

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Callouts
Callouts are first-class Markdown (no package):
::: {.callout-tip}
Base-R `penguins` (R ≥ 4.5) needs no install.
:::






Tip


Base-R penguins (R ≥ 4.5) needs no install.





Do: render one callout live — no package, pure Markdown.
Say: “Five types — note, tip, warning, caution, important — same syntax, different color.”
Frame: next slide closes the live build — inline code.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Inline code
Inline code drops a computed value straight into prose. Put it in a sentence:
We measured `{r} nrow(penguins)` penguins.

It renders with the live count: “We measured 342 penguins.”


The number updates when the data does. Reproducible by construction.


Do: show inline code reporting nrow(penguins) from the data — “the number updates when the data does. Reproducible by construction.”
Closes the live build — next we step back to layout.

title: Introduction to Quarto
Introduction to Quarto
text:
Put output in the margin
A cell’s #| column: margin drops its output (figure, caption, and all) into the margin:
#| column: margin
#| fig-cap: "Bill length by species."
# a margin figure — caption and all
In the lab you’ll use margin layout, the one that does the most for an article. The rest are yours to explore in the worked report.
Learn more: Article Layout · Margin content


Say: “Margin figures still take @fig-/@tbl- — so layout pairs naturally with cross-refs.”

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Make it accessible
Accessibility is a few habits layered on what you already write:

Alt text — you already add #| fig-alt: to every figure; it’s what a screen reader announces.
Color-blind-safe colors — the default palette isn’t. Reach for Okabe-Ito (scale_color_okabe_ito()) or viridis, and encode by shape/label too, not color alone.
Check contrast — WCAG wants 4.5:1 on text. Quarto’s built-in axe runs axe-core on the rendered page: axe: true logs to dev-tools, axe: {output: document} writes the report onto the page itself.

Learn more: HTML Accessibility


Hook: your reader might be on a projector in a bright room, have red-green color-vision deficiency (~8% of men), or use a screen reader — the same few habits cover all three.
Tie to their plot: the penguins scatter defaults to non-safe colors; one line, scale_color_okabe_ito(), fixes it (the worked report already uses it) — show before/after if time.
axe: it’s axe-core (the industry-standard checker), built into Quarto since 1.8 for html/revealjs/dashboard; it runs in the browser on preview and logs to dev-tools — a check-as-you-go tool, not a render/publish gate. Quarto 1.10 polishes the on-page report.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
One source → many formats
One key in the header picks the output. The content stays put:


format: [html, typst]     # render several at once
toc: true                 # shared — applies to both
format:                   # …or set options per format
  html:
    toc: false
  typst:
    toc: true


Shared vs. per-format — top-level keys (toc, number-sections, …) apply to every format; the format: map overrides them per output.
Conditional content — show or hide per format with ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}.
The layout idioms adapt per format: write once, target many.


Learn more: Multiple formats · Conditional content

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: Execution: set once, override per cell
text:
Execution: set once, override per cell
R Markdown’s knitr::opts_chunk$set() moves into the header. Set defaults once, override per cell:


Header — defaults for every cell:
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false

A cell — overrides locally with #|:
#| echo: true
summary(penguins$body_mass)

The header sets the defaults; a cell’s #| wins.
freeze commits computed results to _freeze/ so a project re-render (or CI without R) skips unchanged documents. That’s the Day 2 story.
Learn more: Execution options · Cell options


Do (live): add execute: / echo: false to the header, re-render — every code block disappears at once. Then drop #| echo: true on one cell — just that one returns. The delta, made visible.
Say: “Same idea as opts_chunk$set(), now declarative YAML — dashes not dots, false not FALSE.”
freeze is a one-line teaser only; the real freeze-vs-cache teach is Day 2.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Running & editing
Drive Quarto from the CLI, in whatever editor you like:
quarto preview report.qmd   # live-reloading preview
quarto render  report.qmd   # one-off render

RStudio, Positron, and VS Code all work. The visual editor (WYSIWYM — what you see is what you mean) is built into the RStudio IDE, and comes to Positron and VS Code through the Quarto extension.
The same quarto render also takes -P name:value: override a document parameter to get one report per sample or species from a single source. (Optional bonus in today’s lab.)



Do: run quarto preview report.qmd live — save an edit, show the browser reload; then quarto render for the one-off.
Say: “Drive it from the CLI, in whatever editor you like — RStudio, Positron, VS Code.”
Params (MENTION, cut-first): mention -P here, where quarto render is on screen — the optional lab bonus does it hands-on (one report per species). Don’t dwell; it isn’t a taught beat.
Timing: keep it brief — the room knows cells and Jenny Bryan covers the IDE. Part 1 lands inside its ~18–20 min budget.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Quarto in Positron
The same quarto preview, from inside the editor: source on the left, live preview on the right. Edit, hit Preview, and it live-reloads.




Say: “The CLI preview you just saw — but driven from inside Positron.”
Do: point at the Source / Visual toggle top-left, the visual editor the previous slide mentioned.
Timing: watch-me, cut-first if Part 1 runs long (Jenny Bryan covers the IDE itself).
(Authoring note, not spoken: the shot is a Python example from the Quarto docs; the workflow is language-agnostic — swap in a local R/penguins capture when available.)



Screenshot from the Quarto documentation.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Your turn







Your turn — regroup in ~45 min


Head to the Lab and start at the Authoring Challenge: author a penguins document with a figure, a cross-referenced table, and margin layout, then render it to HTML, then a break, back after.




You can now author a figure, a cross-referenced table, and margin layout. After the break we cite it and ship a branded PDF.


Say (handoff): “Over to you — Authoring Challenge in the lab, ~45 min. Then we break — back at 15:30. Helpers are around; raise your hand if you’re stuck.”
Helpers: most common trap is the cross-ref prefix — a label must start fig-/tbl-/eq-, or @ref renders a stray ?@. Also check the #| lines are the very top of the cell (no blank line or code above them), and watch for duplicate labels across the document.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
From report to article
You have a clean HTML document. The lab ships a Part-2 starter if you need one. To make it a publication-ready article, two more things:

citations — a .bib file and a citation style;
a typeset PDF — via Typst, bundled in Quarto.


This is exactly the path from your analysis to a submission, and to your team-project write-up.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Citations







Follow along


Back in your editor: we add citations to the Part-1 document (or the lab’s starter.qmd).




Point the header at a .bib, then cite with @key:


bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
The data come from Palmer Station
[@gorman2014].
renders as: … Palmer Station (Gorman et al., 2014).



references.bib

@article{gorman2014,
  author  = {Gorman, K. B. and ...},
  title   = {Ecological Sexual ...},
  journal = {PLoS ONE},
  year    = {2014}
}


The reference list renders at the end automatically, or wherever you drop this div:
::: {#refs}
:::



Do: point the header at references.bib + a csl:, drop [@gorman2014] into a sentence, re-render — the in-text cite resolves and a reference list appears at the end.
Say: “One .bib key in your prose becomes a formatted citation and an auto-built reference list — swap the csl: file and the whole style changes.”
Helpers: the .bib path is relative to the document — the follow-along file must sit in day1-intro/ next to references.bib/apa.csl. A [?] in the text means a wrong @key, or bibliography: not set in the header.



CSL = Citation Style Language: the file that decides how citations and the reference list are formatted (APA, Vancouver, a journal’s own style). Swap the csl: file, restyle everything.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
A real title block
A few header lines turn the document into a publication-ready article (name, affiliation, ORCID, abstract):
title: "Bill shape distinguishes Antarctic penguins"
author:
  - name: Christophe Dervieux
    affiliation: Posit, PBC
    email: cderv@posit.co
    orcid: 0000-0003-4474-2498
abstract: |
  Using base-R `penguins`, we show bill shape separates species...
Renders in HTML, PDF, and Typst. Write it once.


Timing (Part-2 trim-first): if Part 2 runs long, this is the slide to cut — name author / affiliation / ORCID / abstract verbally and move on. Citations, Typst, and brand are the must-keeps.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Typst — modern PDF, no LaTeX
Typst is a modern typesetting system that ships inside Quarto: nothing to install, no LaTeX toolchain.
format: typst
That is the whole switch. Then re-render:
quarto render report.qmd --to typst







Pre-flight


Typst is bundled from Quarto 1.4+; we require ≥ 1.9 (margin/article layout). Check once with quarto --version.






Say: “Typst is deterministic and bundled — nothing to install. LaTeX is still there if you need it, but Typst is what we use in 2026.”
Gloss “Typst” on first use.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Branding the PDF — _brand.yml
One _brand.yml carries your palette + fonts to the Typst PDF you just built, and to the plots and tables inside it:




_brand.yml

color:
  palette:
    teal: "#4C979F"
  primary: teal
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Albert Sans
      source: google
  base:
    family: Albert Sans



Same file themes HTML and Typst.
The R side (theme_brand_ggplot2() / theme_brand_gt() from the brand.yml package) themes your plots and tables from the same palette.
Quarto fetches Google fonts for Typst automatically.




Do: add _brand.yml (palette + fonts) and re-render the Typst PDF — colors and type change from that one file. This is the payoff.
Say: “One file themes the PDF — and theme_brand_ggplot2() / _gt() pull the same palette into your plots and tables. Tomorrow the same file will brand a whole project.”
Helpers: a plot won’t inherit the palette until you add a theme_brand_* helper; the first Typst render fetches the Google fonts, so it needs network once.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Your turn







Your turn — regroup in ~30 min


Back to the Lab, at the Citations Challenge: add citations to the Part-2 starter (or your own Part-1 file), then render it as a branded Typst PDF. You’ll finish with a publication-ready article, a cite-able, branded PDF you could submit.






Say (handoff): “Last part — Citations Challenge: add a .bib, render a branded Typst PDF, and you leave with a publication-ready article — a branded, cite-able PDF. ~30 min; helpers are around.”
Helpers: the .bib key must match @key exactly; the Typst Google-font fetch needs network on the first render; a missing csl: falls back to Typst’s native style. “Where’s my PDF?” — in day1-intro/ it lands next to its source (starter.qmd → starter.pdf, my-report.qmd → my-report.pdf), no _site/ redirect. All covered by the lab’s hint/solution.

title: Introduction to Quarto
Introduction to Quarto
text:
Thank you!
Questions?
Learn more: quarto.org/docs/guide · Typst format · _brand.yml

Slides + lab: this site · Christophe Dervieux · GitHub @cderv · cderv@posit.co

title: Introduction to Quarto — Lab
text:
NoteScope



Build one penguins document with the authoring extras, then cite it and render it as a branded Typst PDF. Two challenges, one document: each is its own hands-on part, with a break between them. This is your manuscript / team-project path, the same route from an analysis to a submittable write-up. Everything runs on base-R datasets::penguins (R ≥ 4.5), so there’s no data to download.
Before you start: work through the Setup page if you haven’t. Its 00-check-setup.R confirms R, Quarto, and the packages this lab uses.
Start every document with this setup (the challenges below assume it):
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(ggokabeito)   # color-blind-safe (Okabe-Ito) scale -- see the Accessibility box

data(penguins)
penguins <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep))

title: Introduction to Quarto — Lab
text:
1 Authoring Challenge

Goal: a penguins report with a cross-referenced figure, a cross-referenced table, a margin element, and a display equation, rendered to HTML.







Note Tasks





Create my-report.qmd inside your open day1-intro/ folder (next to references.bib / apa.csl, so Part 2’s paths and branding resolve later) with format: html and the setup cell at the top of this page.
Add a scatter plot of bill_len versus bill_dep colored by species. Give its cell #| label: fig-bill and a #| fig-cap:, then refer to it with @fig-bill in the prose, outside the cell.
Add a summary table. The gt plumbing is below. Your job is the cross-reference mechanic: give the cell #| label: tbl-summary and a #| tbl-cap:, then refer to it with @tbl-summary.
penguins |>
  summarise(bill_len = mean(bill_len), bill_dep = mean(bill_dep), .by = species) |>
  gt()
Put the species counts in the margin with the cell option #| column: margin.
(stretch) Add the bill-shape ratio as a display equation, referenced with @eq-ratio. Escape the underscores: inside $$…$$, bill_len may render as a subscript (depending on the math renderer), so write:
$$
\text{ratio} = \frac{\text{bill\_len}}{\text{bill\_dep}}
$$ {#eq-ratio}
Render to HTML (quarto render my-report.qmd, or the editor’s Render/Preview).




 Quarto docs
Cross-references · Article layout






Tip Make it accessible



The worked report does all three. Do the same in yours:

add a #| fig-alt: to every figure;
add scale_color_okabe_ito() (from ggokabeito) to your plot, keeping shape = species;
add axe: {output: document} under format: html, re-preview, and a WCAG report appears on the page (drop it again before you publish). See Quarto’s accessibility docs.









Note You should see



A numbered Figure 1 (the bill scatter, three separate clusters), a numbered Table 1, the counts sitting in the right margin, and an Equation 1, with @fig-bill / @tbl-summary / @eq-ratio rendering as live “Figure 1” / “Table 1” / “Equation 1” links. Your finished figure looks like this:










Figure 1: Target: bill length versus depth by species.











TipHint






A cell becomes a cross-referenceable figure/table only when its label starts with fig- / tbl- / eq- and is unique in the document.
column: margin is a cell option (#|) for a cell, or a ::: {.column-margin} div for prose.
Display math with a label $$ … $$ {#eq-ratio}, referenced with @eq-ratio.




The complete, runnable solution is starter.qmd, a known-good Part-1 report with all these cells. It’s already in your day1-intro/ folder; open it there to compare, or take the source:

 starter.qmd
The cross-references and the equation live in the body Markdown, outside any cell:
@fig-bill shows bill shape by species; @tbl-summary gives the per-species means.

$$
\text{ratio} = \frac{\text{bill\_len}}{\text{bill\_dep}}
$$ {#eq-ratio}
solutions/day1/penguins-report.qmd is a reference, not a checklist. The complete worked document goes beyond the tasks (a margin culmen figure, a glimpse, section labels) and also adds the citations from the next challenge. It’s in your exercises solutions/day1/ folder. Try the challenge first, then open it to compare, or take the source:

 penguins-report.qmd

title: Introduction to Quarto — Lab
text:
2 Citations Challenge

Goal: cite the report, then render the same document as a branded Typst PDF.







NoteStarting point



If you finished the Authoring Challenge, keep going on your own document. Otherwise open day1-intro/starter.qmd in your editor (a known-good Part-1 report) and add the citations to that.








Note Tasks





Point the document header at the shared bibliography and citation style:
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
Cite the data source in prose with @gorman2014. Find (or add) the sentence ending “…collected at Palmer Station, Antarctica.” and insert the citation before the period: Antarctica [@gorman2014]. (don’t paste a second copy).
Add a References section where the list should appear:
## References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::
Give it a real title block so the PDF reads as a paper. Replace your document’s author: line with:
author:
  - name: Your Name
    affiliation: Your Lab, Your University
Render to HTML and confirm the citation resolves to (Gorman et al., 2014) with a formatted reference list.
Switch the output to Typst and render a branded PDF. (You’ll see a stack of unknown font family warnings as it renders. They’re harmless: the Troubleshooting box below explains them.) Two routes:

CLI — leave the header as-is and force the target:
quarto render your-doc.qmd --to typst
Editor Render button — set format: typst in the YAML header first, then click Render. The button renders whatever format: is declared, so while the header still says format: html the button gives you HTML, not a PDF.

Where the PDF lands: right next to its source in day1-intro/. There’s no project folder above to redirect it, so starter.qmd gives starter.pdf, my-report.qmd gives my-report.pdf.




 Quarto docs
Citations · Typst






Note You should see



In-text (Gorman et al., 2014), a References section formatted in APA, and, in the Typst PDF, the same citation and reference list, typeset with the RaukR palette. No ?@gorman2014 or [?] markers anywhere.








TipHint






The @key in [@gorman2014] must match a key in references.bib exactly.
csl: sets the style (here APA). Swap the file to restyle every citation at once.
Typst reads the .bib itself, so keep bibliography fields plain (avoid LaTeX macros like \emph{} in titles).
On the first Typst render, Quarto downloads the brand’s Google fonts; give it a moment and a network connection.










NoteSolution: the header and the cite





In the YAML header:
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
In prose:
The data come from Palmer Station, Antarctica [@gorman2014].
A References section (the list renders inside the #refs div):
## References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::
For the branded PDF (the project _brand.yml styles it), either force the target from the CLI:
quarto render your-doc.qmd --to typst
or set format: typst in the header and use the editor’s Render button.



The complete cited HTML is solutions/day1/penguins-report.qmd. The branded Typst PDF (with R-side theme_brand_* styling) is day1-intro/sample-typst.qmd (render it to see the branded PDF payoff).

title: Introduction to Quarto — Lab
text:
3 Bonus — one report per species (optional)

Goal: turn a report into a parameterized one: a single source that renders a separate report per species by passing the species in at render time. This is the “one QC report per sample / one summary per cohort” pattern. Fully optional, so skip it if you’re short on time.

A parameter is a value declared in the YAML that your code can read as params$…. Change the value at render time and the same document produces a different report. No copy-paste.






NoteStarting point



The fastest path: open the shipped penguins-by-species.qmd (in your day1-intro/ folder), a complete parameterized report, and just render it for different species (Task 5). Want to build it yourself instead? Add the pieces below to a copy of your Part-1 report, and point your figure/table cells at the filtered one (not penguins) so they track the parameter too.








Note Tasks





Declare a parameter with a default in the header:
params:
  species: Gentoo
Use it to filter in your setup cell. params$species is just a value (keep the same NA guard as the rest of the lab), then plot one instead of penguins:
one <- penguins |> filter(species == params$species, !is.na(bill_len), !is.na(bill_dep))
Build a heading from the parameter with #| output: asis (it writes the cell’s text output as raw Markdown, so cat() becomes a real heading):
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cat("##", params$species, "at a glance\n")
```
Make the caption (and the alt text) track the parameter with !expr. Cell options are YAML, so to run R there you tag the value !expr (and keep a fig-alt, always):
#| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Bill length versus depth for ", params$species, " penguins.")
#| fig-alt: !expr paste0("Scatter plot of bill depth against bill length for ", params$species, " penguins.")
Render a different species from the CLI: same quarto render you used for the Typst PDF, with -P name:value (no Render button for this, since the parameter override is command-line only). Run it from inside day1-intro/:
quarto render penguins-by-species.qmd -P species:Adelie
quarto render penguins-by-species.qmd -P species:Chinstrap
With no -P, the default (Gentoo) is used. The HTML lands next to the source in day1-intro/, as penguins-by-species.html.




 Quarto docs
Parameters






Note You should see



Rendering with -P species:Adelie gives a report whose title sentence, section heading, figure caption, and point count are all about Adelie. Nothing says Gentoo. Change the one word after species: and the whole report follows.








TipHint






Parameters must have defaults: params$species has to resolve when no -P is passed.
-P takes name:value (-P species:Adelie). Pass several with repeated -P flags.
#| output: asis is what lets code emit Markdown (a heading here); without it, cat() output would show as a printed code result, not a heading.




The complete, runnable solution is penguins-by-species.qmd. It’s in your day1-intro/ folder. Open it and render with different -P species: values, or take the source:

 penguins-by-species.qmd

title: Introduction to Quarto — Lab
text:
4 Troubleshooting






Tip If a render misbehaves






YAML is indentation-sensitive. If rendering fails before any code runs, check the YAML header for stray spaces, tabs, or unmatched quotes.
Missing package? install.packages("<name>") (or renv::restore()) and render again.
A figure doesn’t appear? Check the path is relative to the .qmd and the filename matches exactly (case included).
A cross-reference shows ?@…? The cell label must start with fig-/tbl-/eq- and be unique, and the @ref must match it.
A citation shows ?@gorman2014 or [?]? The @key doesn’t match a key in references.bib, or bibliography: isn’t set.
Do I need to install Typst? No. Typst is bundled in Quarto ≥ 1.9, so there’s nothing extra to install (no LaTeX either). Check quarto --version.
Typst PDF looks unbranded / wrong fonts? Confirm _brand.yml is in your day1-intro/ folder (next to the .qmd) and you have network on the first render (Quarto fetches the Google fonts once).
Typst prints unknown font family warnings? Harmless: a plain gt table emits them for its default font stack, and the PDF still builds. (The fully brand-styled table via theme_brand_* is in sample-typst.qmd.)
Prefer to stay in HTML first? Render HTML, get it right, then switch to format: typst. The content is the same.
